The copyright and cataloguing page of the Arabic edition of WHO's Global strategy on digital health 2020–2025, with ISBNs and Creative Commons licence terms. It sets out conditions for reuse and translation, notes on designations and trade names, and a disclaimer of liability; some Latin-script text is garbled in the extraction.

The table of contents of the Arabic edition of the global digital health strategy, listing the acknowledgements, vision, purpose, guiding principles, four strategic objectives, framework for action, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, glossary and annex.

Acknowledgements for the global digital health strategy, describing two years of drafting and consultation, including a 2019 public consultation, regional committee discussions and review by the Executive Board in February 2020 before adoption by the Seventy-third World Health Assembly. It then begins a long list of contributors by name.

Continues the acknowledgements, thanking WHO collaborating centres, UN bodies, private sector representatives, Member State delegates and the technical advisory group on digital health, and lists further named contributors.

Traces the background to the digital health strategy, from Assembly resolution WHA58.28 on eHealth in 2005, after which over 120 countries adopted eHealth strategies, to resolution WHA66.24 on eHealth standardization and interoperability in 2013. It goes on to later Assembly decisions on digital health and the request for a global strategy. The page ends with footnote references, partly garbled in the extraction, including the WHO–ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Explains how digital technologies are shaping global health, citing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and UN General Assembly resolutions on information and communication technologies. It notes growing consensus that digital health is key to WHO's triple billion targets under the Thirteenth General Programme of Work 2019–2023.

Notes that digital transformation can be disruptive but that technologies such as the internet of things, telemedicine, artificial intelligence, big data and wearables can improve health. It refers to WHO's guideline with ten evidence-based recommendations on digital interventions and states that digital health must be ethical, safe, secure, equitable and sustainable.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Sets out the strategy's vision of better health for everyone through person-centred, affordable, scalable and sustainable digital health solutions, including for epidemic preparedness and use of health data. It notes that national strategies are key but hard to realise in low- and middle-income countries and encourages exploring global solutions and shared services.

States the purpose of the global strategy: to strengthen health systems through digital health technologies for consumers, health professionals, providers and industry. It stresses that all Member States, including those with limited access, should benefit, and that an interoperable ecosystem is needed for safe exchange of health data.

Encourages sharing health data with patient consent within a trusted, person-centred ecosystem that protects privacy and security, for both care and secondary uses such as research. It explains that the strategy aims to support international cooperation and national programmes towards universal health coverage and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals within 2020–2025.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Introduces the four guiding principles of the strategy, starting with the need for countries to commit to institutionalizing digital health in national health systems and to pursue an integrated strategy. It also covers promoting appropriate use of digital technologies as digital public goods so that no one is left behind.

Continues the guiding principles, calling for protection against misinformation or infodemics, misuse of health data and rights violations, and stressing digital determinants of health such as literacy and connectivity. It also recognises the need to address major barriers facing least-developed countries, such as infrastructure, skills, investment and connectivity.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Introduces the four strategic objectives and describes the first, promoting global collaboration and transfer of knowledge on digital health. It notes the need for norms, standards and regulations to ensure the quality and safety of digital health products, including those sold directly to consumers.

Lists proposed policy options and actions under strategic objective 1, such as joining in the strategy's development, knowledge management to share good practice and evidence, multistakeholder meetings and national, regional and global disease surveillance information centres.

Describes strategic objective 2, advancing implementation of national digital health strategies through a multistakeholder approach suited to each country's context. It stresses building capacity and a workforce able to use digital technologies, including leadership and skilled health and technology staff.

Lists policy options under strategic objective 2, such as adopting or reviewing national digital health strategies, involving institutions and end users, securing sustainable funding and managing change. It begins listing expected outputs, including a national digital health strategy integrated into the national health strategy.

Completes the outputs of objective 2, including a digital health maturity assessment, and introduces strategic objective 3 on strengthening digital health governance at global, regional and national levels. It mentions a research and testing agenda and begins listing policy options for governance.

Lists further governance options under objective 3, such as sustainable governance structures and regulatory frameworks, coordinated investment in health technology assessment and a national digital health architecture with standards, legal requirements and political engagement.

Lists global guidance on digital hospitals, digital trials and therapeutics as outputs of objective 3, then introduces strategic objective 4 on people-centred health systems enabled by digital health. It highlights digital health literacy, gender equality, patient engagement and evidence-based self-management tools.

Lists policy options under objective 4, such as putting people at the centre through ownership of health data, population health management through digital applications, public participation in decisions, open online training and an international awareness campaign.

Lists expected outputs of objective 4, including better digital health literacy, a feedback framework for digital tools, minimum global health data standards and global guidance on personalized medicine.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Describes the framework for action, which offers structures and tools for partners to collaborate on implementing the strategy. It explains that the WHO Secretariat will promote cooperation and develop shared, evidence-based global digital public goods.

Describes the measure and the improve-and-iterate elements of the framework, under which the Secretariat will assess the strategy's effectiveness and report to Member States and review the action plan yearly.

Opens the section on implementing the strategy and action plan, stating its intended impact in supporting countries towards universal health coverage, the health-related SDGs and WHO's general programme of work. It lists the many stakeholders expected to take part, from intergovernmental bodies to non-state actors.

Continues the list of stakeholders and notes that the actions for 2020–2025 need timelines. It explains that each Member State should weigh its priorities, current digital health status, resources and risks, and that options will vary with the maturity level a country aims for.

Sets out specific implementation principles, urging Member States to choose the most suitable and cost-effective policies. It stresses legal bases for people's access to and consent over their health data, with accountability and protection against unauthorised processing.

Calls for protection against loss or misuse of health data and for trusted digital identity mechanisms for all participants in an interoperable digital health ecosystem. It also calls for a coordinated global approach to the economics of health data use.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Describes monitoring and evaluation of the strategy, asking Member States and the Secretariat to track digital health maturity and assess implementation using agreed standard measures. It recommends that Member States adopt internationally recognised indicators linked to the four strategic objectives.
A photo credit page with no other content.

Opens the glossary of the digital health strategy, defining terms such as appropriate use of digital technologies, artificial intelligence, big data, blockchain, digital divide and digital health. It quotes an earlier definition of digital health as an umbrella term covering eHealth and advanced computing fields.

Continues the glossary with terms such as digital hospital, digital public goods, digital trials, eHealth, enterprise architecture and health data. Footnote references at the end are badly garbled in the extraction.

Continues the glossary with terms such as health information system, ICD-11, infodemic, internet of things, interoperability and multistakeholder groups. Parts of the page contain garbled Latin-script fragments.

Ends the glossary with the list of stakeholders, an interoperable national digital health ecosystem and telemedicine, followed by a reference to WHO's second global eHealth survey report on telemedicine.
A photo credit page with no other content.
The title page of the annex listing proposed actions for Member States, the Secretariat and partners to implement the global strategy on digital health.

Sets out proposed short-term actions under strategic objective 1 for Member States and the Secretariat, such as building partnerships, sharing research gaps and priorities and creating governance bodies for digital health. It also includes knowledge management on the role of digital health investment and a global repository of digital health knowledge.

Continues the proposed actions for objective 1, including multistakeholder meetings on scaling up digital health and emergency preparedness, joining the UN Secretary-General's coalition on digital inclusion and building a knowledge repository. It also covers capacity-building tools, benchmarking frameworks and strategies on ethics, legal frameworks, privacy and data sharing.

Lists proposed actions for partners under objective 1, such as collaborating with countries and the Secretariat, joining partnerships to accelerate digital transformation and building capacity to share good practice. In the long term it proposes centres of excellence or innovation to assess and adapt digital health solutions.

Sets out proposed Member State actions under strategic objective 2, such as stakeholder analysis, assessing connectivity and devices, national coordination mechanisms and national digital health strategies. It also includes using maturity assessment tools, a resilient national digital health architecture and policies on payment and accreditation of digital services.

Lists proposed Secretariat actions under objective 2, such as sharing good practice through networks, supporting countries to develop national strategies and prioritise investment, and attending to quality, safety and ethics. It also proposes a digital platform for health ministries to review solutions and a business-case model within the maturity assessment.

Lists proposed actions for partners under objective 2, mainly collaborating with WHO to support national strategies, prioritise investment in primary care and universal coverage, and develop tools to monitor implementation across development contexts.

Sets out proposed actions for Member States and the Secretariat under strategic objective 3 on governance, such as mapping national start-ups, planning digital health use for health system strengthening and emergencies and building training capacity. It also includes tracking the global digital health ecosystem and research to support Member States.

Lists proposed actions for partners under objective 3, such as supporting registration and coordination of digital investments like WHO's digital health atlas and producing evidence-based technical documents on cost, ethics, privacy and safety. It also proposes a regulatory framework for AI-based medical devices and digital health technologies.
Lists further partner actions under objective 3, supporting the Secretariat on global interoperability standards and on training surge capacity for severe public health crises.

Sets out proposed actions for Member States and the Secretariat under strategic objective 4 on people-centred health systems, such as accessible tools for digital health literacy and engaging professional and patient groups and civil society. It also covers building public trust, supporting personalized medicine and gathering evidence on how digital health affects health systems and people-centred outcomes.

Part of the Arabic annex to the Global strategy on digital health 2020–2025, listing proposed actions for partners under strategic objective 4 on people-centred health systems. Actions span the short, medium and long term, such as global guidance on personalized medicine, ethics frameworks for health technologies, digital literacy tools and feedback frameworks for digital tools.
